name: Literature
description: Novels, plays, poems and the authors who wrote them.

lessons.title: Literary Terms Every Reader Needs
lessons.body:
Quiz bowl literature questions often describe *how* a story is written. Knowing these words helps you understand clues and answer term questions.

## Story parts
- **Plot**: the events of a story. The **climax** is the turning point of highest tension; the **resolution** ties up loose ends.
- **Protagonist**: the main character. **Antagonist**: the character or force working against the protagonist.
- **Setting**: when and where a story happens.
- **Theme**: the big message or idea, such as "friendship is worth sacrifice."
- **Point of view**: **first person** uses "I"; **third person** uses "he," "she" or "they."
- **Foreshadowing**: hints about what will happen later.

## Figurative language
- **Simile**: compares using *like* or *as* ("brave as a lion").
- **Metaphor**: compares directly ("the classroom was a zoo").
- **Personification**: gives human traits to non-human things ("the wind whispered").
- **Alliteration**: repeated starting sounds ("Peter Piper picked").
- **Onomatopoeia**: words that sound like what they mean ("buzz," "sizzle").
- **Hyperbole**: extreme exaggeration ("I've told you a million times").
- **Irony**: the opposite of what is expected.

## Poetry forms
- **Haiku**: Japanese form with lines of **5, 7 and 5 syllables**.
- **Sonnet**: **14 lines**, often in iambic pentameter.
- **Limerick**: a funny five-line poem with an AABBA rhyme.
keyFacts: A simile uses 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor compares directly.
A haiku has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables.
A sonnet has 14 lines.
The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist opposes them.
Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound, like 'buzz'.

lessons.title: Shakespeare’s Greatest Hits
lessons.body:
William **Shakespeare** (1564–1616) wrote about 37 plays and 154 sonnets. Many of his plays were performed at the **Globe Theatre** in London.

## Tragedies
- **Romeo and Juliet:** feuding families, the Montagues and Capulets, in Verona.
- **Hamlet:** a Danish prince avenges his father, murdered by his uncle Claudius. (“To be, or not to be.”)
- **Macbeth:** three witches predict a Scottish general will be king; Lady Macbeth urges murder.

## Comedies
- **A Midsummer Night’s Dream:** fairies Oberon and Titania, and Puck turns Bottom’s head into a donkey’s.
- **The Tempest:** the magician Prospero on an island with Ariel and Caliban.

**Quiz bowl tip:** questions about plays love **character names**. Knowing that Mercutio and Tybalt are from *Romeo and Juliet*, or Banquo from *Macbeth*, earns early buzzes.
keyFacts: Romeo and Juliet are from the feuding Montague and Capulet families.
Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark; his uncle is Claudius.
Three witches tell Macbeth he will be king; Banquo is his friend.
Puck gives Bottom a donkey’s head in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.
Prospero is the magician in The Tempest.

lessons.title: Great British Novels
lessons.body:
British novels from the 1800s and 1900s are some of the most common quiz bowl answers.

- **Charles Dickens** wrote about poor children and London life: **Oliver Twist** ("Please, sir, I want some more"), **A Christmas Carol** (Ebenezer **Scrooge**, Tiny Tim, Marley's ghost), **Great Expectations** (the orphan **Pip** and Miss Havisham) and **A Tale of Two Cities** ("It was the best of times, it was the worst of times," set in London and Paris during the French Revolution).
- **Jane Austen** wrote **Pride and Prejudice**, about Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy.
- **Mary Shelley** wrote **Frankenstein** (1818). Victor Frankenstein is the scientist, *not* the creature.
- **Robert Louis Stevenson** wrote **Treasure Island** (Jim Hawkins and pirate Long John Silver) and **Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde**.
- **Arthur Conan Doyle** created detective **Sherlock Holmes**, who lives at 221B Baker Street with Dr. Watson.
- **George Orwell** wrote **Animal Farm** (pigs Napoleon and Snowball take over a farm; "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others") and **1984** (Big Brother is watching you).
- **William Golding** wrote **Lord of the Flies**: boys stranded on an island, with Ralph, Piggy, Jack and a conch shell.

**Tip:** Dickens questions often start with minor characters. Learn one side character per book.
keyFacts: Ebenezer Scrooge is the miser in A Christmas Carol.
Pip is the orphan hero of Great Expectations.
Victor Frankenstein is the scientist; the creature has no name.
Sherlock Holmes lives at 221B Baker Street.
In Animal Farm, the pig Napoleon becomes a dictator.
Ralph and Piggy use a conch shell in Lord of the Flies.

lessons.title: Classic American Novels
lessons.body:
These novels show up again and again in middle school quiz bowl.

- **The Adventures of Tom Sawyer** and **Adventures of Huckleberry Finn** by **Mark Twain** (real name Samuel Clemens). Huck rafts down the Mississippi with Jim, who is escaping slavery.
- **Little Women** by **Louisa May Alcott**: the March sisters Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy.
- **The Call of the Wild** by **Jack London**: Buck, a dog taken to the Yukon during the Klondike Gold Rush.
- **To Kill a Mockingbird** by **Harper Lee**: Scout Finch, her father Atticus, and the mysterious Boo Radley.
- **The Outsiders** by **S. E. Hinton**: Ponyboy Curtis and the Greasers versus the Socs. Hinton started it at age 15.
keyFacts: Mark Twain’s real name was Samuel Clemens.
Jo March is the main character of Little Women.
Buck is the dog in The Call of the Wild.
Atticus Finch is Scout’s father in To Kill a Mockingbird.
Ponyboy Curtis narrates The Outsiders.

lessons.title: American Classics: Hawthorne to Steinbeck
lessons.body:
These American books show up at every level of quiz bowl.

- **Washington Irving**: **"The Legend of Sleepy Hollow"** (schoolteacher **Ichabod Crane** and the Headless Horseman) and **"Rip Van Winkle"**, who sleeps for 20 years.
- **Nathaniel Hawthorne**: **The Scarlet Letter**. In Puritan Boston, **Hester Prynne** must wear a red letter **"A."** Her daughter is Pearl.
- **Herman Melville**: **Moby-Dick**. It begins "Call me Ishmael." **Captain Ahab** of the ship *Pequod* hunts a white whale that took his leg.
- **John Steinbeck**: **Of Mice and Men** (George and Lennie dream of owning a farm) and **The Grapes of Wrath** (the Joad family flees the Dust Bowl for California).
- **F. Scott Fitzgerald**: **The Great Gatsby**, narrated by **Nick Carraway**. Jay Gatsby stares at a **green light** across the water.
- **Ray Bradbury**: **Fahrenheit 451**. Fireman **Guy Montag** burns books; the title is the temperature at which paper supposedly burns.
- **Jack London**: **White Fang** (the opposite journey of *The Call of the Wild*: a wild wolf-dog becomes tame).
keyFacts: Hester Prynne wears a scarlet 'A' in The Scarlet Letter.
Moby-Dick begins 'Call me Ishmael'; Captain Ahab hunts the whale.
George and Lennie are the friends in Of Mice and Men.
Nick Carraway narrates The Great Gatsby.
Guy Montag is the book-burning fireman in Fahrenheit 451.

lessons.title: American Poets
lessons.body:
Poetry questions usually quote a famous line or describe a poem's subject.

- **Robert Frost** (New England): **"The Road Not Taken"** ("Two roads diverged in a yellow wood") and **"Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening"** ("And miles to go before I sleep"). He read a poem at John F. Kennedy's inauguration.
- **Emily Dickinson** (Amherst, Massachusetts): wrote nearly 1,800 short poems full of **dashes**, but fewer than a dozen were published while she lived. Famous lines: "Because I could not stop for Death," and "'Hope' is the thing with feathers."
- **Edgar Allan Poe**: **"The Raven"**, where a bird repeats "**Nevermore**." He also wrote spooky stories like **"The Tell-Tale Heart"** and is called the father of the detective story.
- **Walt Whitman**: **Leaves of Grass** and **"O Captain! My Captain!"**, a poem mourning **Abraham Lincoln**. He wrote in **free verse** (no regular rhyme or meter).
- **Henry Wadsworth Longfellow**: **"Paul Revere's Ride"** ("Listen, my children, and you shall hear") and **The Song of Hiawatha**.
- **Langston Hughes**: leader of the **Harlem Renaissance**. His poem "Harlem" asks, "What happens to a dream deferred?"
- **Maya Angelou**: "Still I Rise" and the memoir **I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings**.
keyFacts: Robert Frost wrote 'The Road Not Taken'.
Emily Dickinson used many dashes and lived in Amherst, Massachusetts.
The raven in Poe's poem says 'Nevermore'.
Walt Whitman's 'O Captain! My Captain!' mourns Abraham Lincoln.
Langston Hughes was a leader of the Harlem Renaissance.

lessons.title: Fantasy and Classic Children's Books
lessons.body:
Many quiz bowl favorites are fantasy stories you may have already read.

- **J. R. R. Tolkien**: **The Hobbit** (Bilbo Baggins, the wizard Gandalf and the dragon **Smaug**) and **The Lord of the Rings** (Frodo carries the One Ring to Mount Doom).
- **C. S. Lewis**: **The Chronicles of Narnia**. In *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe*, the four **Pevensie** children (Peter, Susan, Edmund, Lucy) enter Narnia through a wardrobe. **Aslan** is the lion; the **White Witch** makes it "always winter and never Christmas."
- **Lewis Carroll**: **Alice's Adventures in Wonderland**: the White Rabbit, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter and the Queen of Hearts ("Off with her head!").
- **L. Frank Baum**: **The Wonderful Wizard of Oz**: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion follow the yellow brick road to the Emerald City. (In the book, her slippers are silver, not ruby.)
- **J. M. Barrie**: **Peter Pan**: Wendy, Tinker Bell, Captain Hook and Neverland.
- **Madeleine L'Engle**: **A Wrinkle in Time**: Meg Murry travels by "tesseract" to rescue her father.
- **Roald Dahl**: **Charlie and the Chocolate Factory**, **Matilda**, **James and the Giant Peach** and **The BFG**.
- **J. K. Rowling**: the **Harry Potter** series, starting at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.
keyFacts: Smaug is the dragon in The Hobbit.
Aslan the lion rules Narnia; the Pevensies enter through a wardrobe.
Lewis Carroll wrote Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
Dorothy's slippers are silver in L. Frank Baum's book.
Meg Murry travels by tesseract in A Wrinkle in Time.
Roald Dahl wrote Matilda and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.

lessons.title: Award-Winning Middle Grade Novels
lessons.body:
Middle school tournaments love books written for readers your age. Many have won the **Newbery Medal**, the top American award for children's books.

| Book | Author | Main character and story |
|---|---|---|
| **The Giver** | Lois Lowry | Jonas becomes the Receiver of Memory in a community without color or pain |
| **Number the Stars** | Lois Lowry | Annemarie helps her Jewish friend Ellen escape Nazi-occupied Denmark |
| **Hatchet** | Gary Paulsen | Brian Robeson survives alone in the Canadian wilderness after a plane crash |
| **Holes** | Louis Sachar | Stanley Yelnats digs holes at Camp Green Lake |
| **Bridge to Terabithia** | Katherine Paterson | Jess and Leslie invent a secret kingdom in the woods |
| **Island of the Blue Dolphins** | Scott O'Dell | Karana lives alone on an island off California |
| **Where the Red Fern Grows** | Wilson Rawls | Billy raises two hounds, Old Dan and Little Ann |
| **Wonder** | R. J. Palacio | Auggie Pullman starts fifth grade after years of homeschooling |
| **Charlotte's Web** | E. B. White | The spider Charlotte saves the pig Wilbur by writing words in her web |

**Tip:** Stanley Yelnats's name is a palindrome: it reads the same backward.
keyFacts: Jonas is the Receiver of Memory in The Giver by Lois Lowry.
Brian Robeson survives with only a hatchet in Gary Paulsen's novel.
Stanley Yelnats digs holes at Camp Green Lake.
Charlotte writes 'Some Pig' in her web to save Wilbur.
The Newbery Medal honors the best American children's book each year.

lessons.title: World Literature
lessons.body:
These books were written outside Britain and the United States but are famous everywhere.

- **Miguel de Cervantes** (Spain): **Don Quixote**. An old man from La Mancha reads too many knight stories, attacks **windmills** thinking they are giants, and rides with his squire **Sancho Panza**.
- **Victor Hugo** (France): **Les Misérables** (ex-convict **Jean Valjean** is chased by Inspector **Javert**) and **The Hunchback of Notre-Dame** (the bell-ringer **Quasimodo** and Esmeralda).
- **Alexandre Dumas** (France): **The Three Musketeers** (d'Artagnan joins Athos, Porthos and Aramis: "All for one, and one for all!") and **The Count of Monte Cristo** (Edmond Dantès escapes prison and takes revenge).
- **Jules Verne** (France): **Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas** (Captain **Nemo** and the submarine *Nautilus*) and **Around the World in Eighty Days** (Phileas Fogg and his servant Passepartout).
- **Hans Christian Andersen** (Denmark): fairy tales like "The Little Mermaid," "The Ugly Duckling" and "The Emperor's New Clothes."
- **The Brothers Grimm** (Germany): collected folk tales such as "Hansel and Gretel" and "Rapunzel."
- **Anne Frank** (Netherlands): **The Diary of a Young Girl**, written while hiding from the Nazis in the "Secret Annex" in Amsterdam.
- **Homer** (ancient Greece): the epic poems the **Iliad** and the **Odyssey**. (See the Mythology lessons for more.)
keyFacts: Don Quixote attacks windmills; his squire is Sancho Panza.
Jean Valjean is chased by Javert in Les Misérables.
Captain Nemo commands the Nautilus in Jules Verne's novel.
Hans Christian Andersen was Danish and wrote 'The Ugly Duckling'.
Anne Frank hid in the Secret Annex in Amsterdam.

tossups.question: In this play, Banquo’s ghost appears at a feast. The title character is told he cannot be harmed by any man “of woman born,” and his wife sleepwalks while trying to wash away imaginary blood. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare tragedy about a Scottish king.

In this novel, a man named Bob Ewell attacks two children on Halloween night. Tom Robinson is defended in court by Atticus Finch in this book. For 10 points, name this Harper Lee novel narrated by Scout.

This device appears in the phrase "the wind howled through the trees," since wind cannot really howl. Robert Frost's woods might "whisper" thanks to this device. For 10 points, name this figure of speech that gives human qualities to non-human things.

Words like "sizzle," "crash" and "buzz" are examples of this device. Comic books use it in sound effects like "POW" and "BAM." For 10 points, name this term for a word that imitates the sound it describes.

Basho wrote a famous one about a frog jumping into an old pond. This form traditionally includes a seasonal word called a kigo. Its three lines have 5, 7 and 5 syllables. For 10 points, name this short Japanese poetry form.

Shakespeare wrote 154 of these poems, and Petrarch popularized an Italian version of them. They are usually written in iambic pentameter, and the Shakespearean kind ends with a rhyming couplet. For 10 points, name this kind of 14-line poem.

In O. Henry's "The Gift of the Magi," a wife sells her hair to buy a watch chain while her husband sells his watch to buy her combs, an example of the situational type of this device. In the dramatic type, the audience knows something a character does not. For 10 points, name this device in which the opposite of what is expected happens.

In this play, the heroine fakes her own death with a potion given to her by Friar Laurence. Mercutio is killed by Tybalt in a street fight in Verona. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare tragedy about two "star-crossed lovers" from the Montague and Capulet families.

This character's friends Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are sent to spy on him. He stages a play called "The Mousetrap" and holds the skull of a jester named Yorick. For 10 points, name this Prince of Denmark who says "To be, or not to be."

In this play, a group of workmen rehearse a play about Pyramus and Thisbe. The fairy king Oberon quarrels with Titania, and the mischievous Puck gives Nick Bottom the head of a donkey. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy set mostly in a forest near Athens.

This play's title character is warned to "beware the Ides of March." Mark Antony gives a speech beginning "Friends, Romans, countrymen," and the dying title character asks "Et tu, Brute?" For 10 points, name this Shakespeare play about a Roman leader stabbed by senators.

In this story, a man is visited by his dead partner Jacob Marley, who is wrapped in chains. He is shown the Cratchit family and the sickly Tiny Tim. For 10 points, name this Charles Dickens story in which Ebenezer Scrooge is visited by three ghosts.

This character was raised by his sister and her husband, the blacksmith Joe Gargery. He helps the escaped convict Magwitch and falls for the cold Estella, who lives with Miss Havisham. For 10 points, name this orphan narrator of Dickens's Great Expectations.

In this novel, the horse Boxer works himself nearly to death and keeps saying "I will work harder." The commandment "Four legs good, two legs bad" is changed after the pigs Napoleon and Snowball take over. For 10 points, name this George Orwell novel about animals that overthrow Farmer Jones.

This character's friend Dr. Watson writes about his adventures, and his archenemy is Professor Moriarty. He solved The Hound of the Baskervilles and lives at 221B Baker Street. For 10 points, name this detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle.

In this novel, a boy's glasses are used to start a fire, and a pig's head on a stick is called the title figure. Ralph is elected leader because he blew a conch shell. For 10 points, name this William Golding novel about schoolboys stranded on an island.

This book's narrator Robert Walton meets a dying man in the Arctic. The man tells how he built a creature from body parts that later kills his brother William and his bride Elizabeth. For 10 points, name this 1818 novel by Mary Shelley.

In this novel, a boy fakes his own death and hides on Jackson's Island. He and a man escaping slavery named Jim float down the Mississippi River on a raft. For 10 points, name this Mark Twain novel narrated by a friend of Tom Sawyer.

In this novel, one sister burns another's manuscript, and the youngest sister, Amy, later marries Laurie. Beth dies of illness, and Jo becomes a writer. For 10 points, name this Louisa May Alcott novel about the four March sisters.

This dog's first owner is Judge Miller in California, but he is stolen and sold. He learns "the law of club and fang," pulls a sled for John Thornton, and finally answers the call of the wolves. For 10 points, name this dog in Jack London's The Call of the Wild.

In this novel, Johnny and Ponyboy hide in an abandoned church after Johnny kills a Soc named Bob. Ponyboy's brothers are Darry and Sodapop. For 10 points, name this S. E. Hinton novel about the Greasers.

This character competes with Brom Bones for the hand of Katrina Van Tassel. After a party, he is chased by a rider who throws a pumpkin at him. For 10 points, name this schoolteacher who flees the Headless Horseman in a Washington Irving story.

This novel's narrator meets the harpooner Queequeg at an inn in New Bedford. Captain Ahab nails a gold coin to the mast of the Pequod. For 10 points, name this Herman Melville novel that begins "Call me Ishmael."

This woman refuses to name the father of her daughter Pearl, who is the minister Arthur Dimmesdale. She is shamed on a scaffold in Puritan Boston. For 10 points, name this heroine of The Scarlet Letter who must wear a red "A."

In this novel, the dog Candy owns is shot because it is old. One character accidentally kills Curley's wife, and the two main characters dream of tending rabbits on their own farm. For 10 points, name this John Steinbeck novel about George and Lennie.

In this novel, the Mechanical Hound hunts people down, and a teenager named Clarisse asks the main character if he is happy. Guy Montag is a fireman who burns books. For 10 points, name this Ray Bradbury novel named for a temperature.

This novel is set in the towns of West Egg and East Egg on Long Island. A billboard shows the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, and the title character stares at a green light at the end of Daisy's dock. For 10 points, name this F. Scott Fitzgerald novel narrated by Nick Carraway.

In this poem, the speaker is "weak and weary" over a "volume of forgotten lore" while mourning the lost Lenore. A bird perches on a bust of Pallas and repeats one word. For 10 points, name this Edgar Allan Poe poem in which a black bird says "Nevermore."

This poet wrote "Mending Wall," which says "Good fences make good neighbors." In another poem, he stops in the woods on "the darkest evening of the year." For 10 points, name this New England poet of "The Road Not Taken."

This poet wrote that "Hope" is "the thing with feathers." Most of her nearly 1,800 poems were found by her sister after she died, and they use lots of dashes. For 10 points, name this poet from Amherst who wrote "Because I could not stop for Death."

This poet wrote "I, Too" and asked "What happens to a dream deferred?" His poem "The Negro Speaks of Rivers" mentions the Euphrates and the Mississippi. For 10 points, name this leading poet of the Harlem Renaissance.

This poet's collection Leaves of Grass includes "Song of Myself." He worked as a nurse during the Civil War and wrote "O Captain! My Captain!" after the death of Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this American poet known for free verse.

In this book, a creature named Gollum asks riddles in the dark and loses a magic ring. The wizard Gandalf sends the title character on a quest with thirteen dwarves to face the dragon Smaug. For 10 points, name this J. R. R. Tolkien book about Bilbo Baggins.
acceptable: The Hobbit, or There and Back Again

tossups.question: In this book, Edmund betrays his siblings for Turkish Delight. Mr. Tumnus the faun meets Lucy, and the White Witch makes it always winter. For 10 points, name this C. S. Lewis book in which the Pevensie children meet the lion Aslan.
tossups.answer: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

tossups.question: In this book, the title character plays croquet with flamingos and meets a caterpillar smoking a hookah. She attends a tea party with the Mad Hatter and the March Hare. For 10 points, name this Lewis Carroll book in which a girl follows a White Rabbit.

In this book, Charles Wallace and Calvin O'Keefe join the main character on a trip to the planet Camazotz, which is ruled by the brain called IT. Mrs. Whatsit explains travel by tesseract. For 10 points, name this Madeleine L'Engle novel about Meg Murry.

In this book, a girl causes a glass of water to tip over with her mind. Her teacher Miss Honey is bullied by the headmistress Miss Trunchbull. For 10 points, name this Roald Dahl novel about a brilliant girl who loves to read.

This novel's main character carries Kate Barlow's lipstick tube and finds a buried chest. He climbs a mountain shaped like a thumb with his friend Zero. For 10 points, name this Louis Sachar novel in which Stanley Yelnats is sent to Camp Green Lake.

This character uses a gift from his mother to make fire from sparks. He survives a moose attack and a tornado after his pilot dies of a heart attack. For 10 points, name this boy who survives in the Canadian wilderness in Gary Paulsen's Hatchet.

In this novel, people take a pill each morning to stop "stirrings," and anyone who breaks the rules is "released." At the Ceremony of Twelve, the main character is chosen to receive memories. For 10 points, name this Lois Lowry novel about Jonas.

In this book, Templeton the rat helps collect words like "Terrific" and "Radiant." Fern Arable saves a runt pig named Wilbur. For 10 points, name this E. B. White book about a spider who writes in her web.

In this novel, a boy runs footraces at recess and shares art lessons with Miss Edmunds. He and his friend Leslie Burke swing on a rope across a creek to reach their imaginary kingdom. For 10 points, name this Katherine Paterson novel about Jess Aarons.

In this novel, a girl's sister Kirsti is given a seashell by a German soldier, and the family pretends a coffin holds Great-aunt Birte. Annemarie helps her friend Ellen Rosen escape to Sweden. For 10 points, name this Lois Lowry novel set in Nazi-occupied Denmark.

This character's horse is named Rocinante, and he chooses a farm girl named Dulcinea as his lady. He attacks windmills, thinking they are giants. For 10 points, name this man from La Mancha who rides with his squire Sancho Panza in a novel by Cervantes.

This character is imprisoned for 19 years for stealing bread and later becomes mayor under the name Monsieur Madeleine. He adopts the orphan Cosette and is hunted by Inspector Javert. For 10 points, name this hero of Victor Hugo's Les Misérables.

This character's submarine runs on electricity and battles a giant squid. Professor Aronnax and the harpooner Ned Land become his prisoners aboard the Nautilus. For 10 points, name this captain created by Jules Verne in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas.

In this novel, a young Gascon arrives in Paris and fights duels against Cardinal Richelieu's guards. He befriends Athos, Porthos and Aramis. For 10 points, name this Alexandre Dumas novel whose heroes shout "All for one, and one for all!"

This author's fairy tales include "The Snow Queen" and "The Steadfast Tin Soldier." In one of his stories, a weavers' trick is exposed when a child shouts that the Emperor is wearing nothing. For 10 points, name this Danish author of "The Ugly Duckling."
